A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEED research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial changes in scope and organization.

before.justification: V1 reports original human evaluations of 1,000 reconstructions, metric comparisons, decoder re-evaluations, ablations and experiments with the proposed pairwise hinge loss.

after.justification: V2 retains original NSD evaluations and adds GOD/Mind-Vis human evaluations, component robustness experiments, statistical analyses and additional failure studies.

M1.justification: V2 removes the separate pairwise hinge-loss method, including its combined training objective and scheduled application from v1 Section 5. Default Object F1, Cap-Sim and SEED computations remain equivalent. V2 Appendix B.2 also introduces an evaluated variant that obtains per-image object categories from Qwen2.5-VL instead of the fixed category list.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates NSD natural-scene reconstructions. V2 additionally evaluates 50 GOD reconstructions generated by Mind-Vis, using GOD's 50 test-class names for object detection (Section 5.2, Table 2). This extends coverage to another corpus within the same visual brain-decoding task.

E2.justification: The baseline-versus-loss comparisons for MindEye2, MindBridge and UniBrain disappear with the training study. V1's standalone BLIP Cap-Sim comparator is also removed from metric meta-evaluation. BLIP/GIT FlanT5 comparisons remain under the names BLIP/GIT VQAScore in v2 Table 5. BrainGuard joins the decoder comparison in Table 6.

E3.justification: V2 adds a GOD protocol with 10 raters and 50 reconstructions, eight component-model configurations, and a semantic-detail-miss criterion using Object F1 > 0.7 and Object F1 - SEED > 0.2. It removes the loss-training and hyperparameter-selection experiments and drops four low-level evaluation metrics from Table 6. The original 22-rater, 1,000-image NSD survey design is retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds dataset/decoder and component-choice robustness tests, fixed-versus-VLM category analysis, semantic-detail-miss analysis, and case studies of failures by existing metrics and SEED itself. Cap-Sim examples are replaced in Figures 4 and 11. The existing location/size/count and metric-combination analyses are retained in Appendix C.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without confidence intervals or rater-agreement statistics. V2 adds ICC estimates for NSD and GOD ratings and 1,000 bootstrap iterations resampling the 22 NSD evaluators, with 95% confidence intervals for SEED-minus-EffNet differences. These are new statistical reporting procedures; the original NSD panel size does not increase.

E6.justification: New results include GOD SEED pairwise accuracy of 73.7% and semantic-detail-miss rates of 8.3–10.7%. Loss-training results and Table 6's low-level scores disappear. Retained results also change: SEED's NSD Pearson correlation goes from .817 to .813, GIT VQA accuracy from 71.5% to 71.7%, and MindBridge's Table 6 SEED score from .410 to .403. V2 inconsistently reports Cap-Sim Pearson as .666 in Table 1 and .683 in Table 5.

T1.justification: Formal changes are limited to removing the pairwise hinge-loss definition and combined objective, and introducing the threshold-based semantic-detail-miss definition. The mathematical definitions underlying Object F1, Cap-Sim and SEED remain equivalent. The added visual-attention discussion supplies conceptual motivation without new formal assumptions or proofs.

C1.justification: V2 removes the abstract, introduction and conclusion claims about a novel loss consistently improving decoding models. It retains SEED's human-alignment claim while foregrounding neuroscientific inspiration and failure diagnosis, including the new claim that reconstructions can preserve objects while losing semantic details.

C2.justification: V2 introduces a visual-attention interpretation of the metric components and expands explanations of semantic-detail failures. It proposes targeted data collection and separate object/detail supervision as possible remedies. Its limitations now address inherited errors from component models and joint failures on distorted images, extending v1's brief warning about perceptual fidelity.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a repository link stated to provide SEED code and human ratings, the Qwen category-generation model and prompt, and details of per-evaluator normalization for rankings. V1's loss implementation, hyperparameter search ranges, reduced MindEye2 configuration, training splits and four-A100 hardware disclosure are removed with the discarded training study.

R1.justification: V2 substantially changes positioning through a two-stage visual-attention rationale citing Jonides, Treisman and Zhang, and explicitly claims that caption-based image-similarity evaluation has not previously been proposed. The background expands coverage of multimodal and brain-to-text decoding and newer systems such as MindTuner and BrainGuard, while shortening the original decoder architecture descriptions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background and conclusion are substantially rewritten. V2 removes the three-contribution bullet list, integrates visual-attention explanations throughout the method presentation, and reorganizes the experimental narrative around validation and failure discovery. The combination discussion moves into Appendix C.3, and the appendices are extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a predominantly single-column ICLR layout, removes the loss-results table and qualitative galleries, and adds GOD/VLM tables and robustness/failure figures. The combination heatmap moves from main Figure 3 to appendix Figure 8; v1 Table 2's findings become prose. Table 6 gains BrainGuard and SDM while losing low-level columns, and several example panels are replaced.

improvement.justification: V1's central human-alignment validation relied on NSD/MindEye2 without reported rater reliability or significance testing. V2's additional GOD/Mind-Vis study, component robustness checks, statistical reporting and explicit joint-failure analysis substantially strengthen support for the metric and clarify its boundaries. Removing the loss contribution narrows scope, and the Cap-Sim discrepancy between Tables 1 and 5 remains a reporting weakness. The gains nevertheless address important deficiencies in validation of the central contribution.
